claim: GABA neurotransmission supports inhibition in the adult brain but excites immature rodent neurons.
source: γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) neurotransmission supports inhibition in the adult brain but excites immature rodent neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about GABA developmental sequence.

claim: Alterations in the timing of the GABA switch contribute to neurological disorders.
source: Alterations in the timing of the GABA switch contribute to neurological disorders, so unveiling the involved regulators may be a promising strategy for treatment.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction referencing studies on ASD, Rett syndrome, Down syndrome, and Huntington's disease.

claim: Leptin sets the tempo for the emergence of GABAergic inhibition in the newborn rodent hippocampus.
source: Here we show that the adipocyte hormone leptin sets the tempo for the emergence of GABAergic inhibition in the newborn rodent hippocampus.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: In the absence of leptin signaling, hippocampal neurons show an advanced emergence of GABAergic inhibition.
source: In the absence of leptin signaling, hippocampal neurons show an advanced emergence of GABAergic inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from db/db and ob/ob mice shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Maternal obesity associated with hyperleptinemia delays the excitatory to inhibitory switch of GABA action in offspring.
source: Conversely, maternal obesity associated with hyperleptinemia delays the excitatory to inhibitory switch of GABA action in offspring.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from diet-induced obese (DIO) dams shown in Figure 4.

claim: In rodents, at fetal and postnatal stages, GABA induces a membrane depolarization due to elevated intracellular chloride concentration.
source: However, in rodents, at fetal and postnatal stages, GABA induces a membrane depolarization due to elevated intracellular chloride concentration ([Cl-]i) (Ben-Ari et al., 2007; Sulis Sato et al., 2017; Owens and Kriegstein, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by three citations to previous studies.

claim: During the second postnatal week of life, the functional expression of KCC2 causes [Cl-]i to decrease and shifts GABAergic responses towards a more hyperpolarized value.
source: During the second postnatal week of life, the functional expression of the chloride extruder, K+-Cl- type 2 co-transporter (KCC2), causes [Cl-]i to decrease and consequently shifts the chloride-dependent GABAergic responses towards a more hyperpolarized value (Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rivera et al., 2015.

claim: The developmental sequence of GABA is likely shifted toward fetal life in humans.
source: This developmental sequence is likely shifted toward fetal life in humans (Chen and Kriegstein, 2015; Sedmak et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by two citations.

claim: Defective chloride homeostasis plays a role in phenotypes associated with autism spectrum disorders.
source: Rodent studies showed that defective chloride homeostasis plays a role in phenotypes associated with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) (Tyzio et al., 2014; He et al., 2014), Rett syndrome (Banerjee et al., 2016; El-Khoury et al., 2014), Down syndrome (Deidda et al., 2015) and Huntington's disease (Dargaei et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to rodent studies.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations aimed at restoring low [Cl-]i improve neurological symptoms in rodents.
source: Conversely, pharmacological manipulations aimed at restoring low [Cl-]i improve neurological symptoms in rodents (Tyzio et al., 2006; Deidda et al., 2015; Banerjee et al., 2016; Dargaei et al., 2018) and humans (Lemonnier et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies in rodents and humans.

claim: Leptin is a 16 kDa cytokine produced and secreted mainly by the adipose tissue.
source: Leptin is a 16 kDa cytokine produced and secreted mainly by the adipose tissue.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about leptin.

claim: In the adult, leptin regulates body weight and reproduction acting on specific hypothalamic nuclei.
source: In the adult, leptin regulates body weight and reproduction acting on specific hypothalamic nuclei (Ahima and Flier, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ahima and Flier, 2000.

claim: Leptin can act beyond its classical role and may function as a neurotrophic signal.
source: However, rodent studies show that leptin can act beyond this classical role and may function as a neurotrophic signal (Bouret, 2010; Harvey, 2013; Guimond et al., 2014; Briffa et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to rodent studies.

claim: In both humans and rodents leptin levels surge during intense period of neuronal growth and synaptogenesis.
source: In both humans and rodents leptin levels surge during intense period of neuronal growth and synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by the developmental profile data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Leptin levels remain elevated in children with early onset ASD.
source: Leptin levels remain elevated in children with early onset ASD (Rodrigues et al., 2014), Rett syndrome (Blardi et al., 2009) and Fragile X syndrome (Lisik et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Maternal obesity which is associated with hyperleptinemia heightens the risk of ASD and other neuropsychiatric disorders in children.
source: Likewise, maternal obesity which is associated with hyperleptinemia heightens the risk of ASD and other neuropsychiatric disorders in children (Wang et al., 2016; Rivera et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by two citations.

claim: Isoguvacine increased the firing of wt CA3 pyramidal neurons from P1 to P6.
source: Consistent with the known depolarizing action of GABA in the newborn hippocampus (Ben-Ari et al., 2007), isoguvacine increased the firing of wt CA3 pyramidal neurons from P1 to P6 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and a citation to Ben-Ari et al., 2007.

claim: In db/db mice, the excitatory action of isoguvacine was only observed at P1.
source: Remarkably, in db/db mice, the excitatory action of isoguvacine was only observed at P1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: As early as P3, isoguvacine decreased the firing of the CA3 pyramidal db/db neurons.
source: As early as P3, isoguvacine decreased the firing of the CA3 pyramidal db/db neurons (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At P15, the effect of isoguvacine on the firing of the CA3 pyramidal neurons was similar in wt and db/db mice.
source: At P15, the effect of isoguvacine on the firing of the CA3 pyramidal neurons was similar in wt and db/db mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In wt CA3 neurons, EGABA shifted from depolarizing to hyperpolarizing values during the second postnatal week of life.
source: In wt CA3 neurons, the reversal potential of eGABAA-PSCs (EGABA) shifted from depolarizing to hyperpolarizing values during the second postnatal week of life (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In db/db neurons, the shift in EGABA occurred earlier, few days after birth.
source: In db/db neurons, this shift occurred earlier, few days after birth (Figure 1D, at P3 EGABA was −38 ± 8 mV in wt and −64 ± 3 mV in db/db neurons, p=0.023, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: The membrane potential at zero current was similar between wt and db/db neurons at all age investigated.
source: In contrast the membrane potential at zero current was similar between wt and db/db neurons at all age investigated (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Circulating leptin levels were low at birth in wt, rose to a peak by the end of the first postnatal week and declined to low levels during the third postnatal week of life.
source: We found that circulating leptin levels were low at birth in wt, rose to a peak by the end of the first postnatal week and declined to low levels during the third postnatal week of life (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The developmental profile of leptin levels paralleled the developmental difference in EGABA observed between wt and db/db neurons.
source: Interestingly, this developmental profile of leptin levels paralleled the developmental difference in EGABA observed between wt and db/db neurons (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: ob/ob mice exhibit an advanced emergence of GABAergic inhibition in vivo.
source: We found that ob/ob mice also exhibit an advanced emergence of GABAergic inhibition in vivo, an effect partially restored by subcutaneous recombinant leptin injections to mimic the leptin surge occurring in wt mice in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subcutaneous recombinant leptin injections partially restored the advanced emergence of GABAergic inhibition in ob/ob mice.
source: We found that ob/ob mice also exhibit an advanced emergence of GABAergic inhibition in vivo, an effect partially restored by subcutaneous recombinant leptin injections to mimic the leptin surge occurring in wt mice in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: KCC2 mRNA levels were enhanced in db/db hippocampi compared to wt at P6.
source: KCC2 mRNA levels were enhanced in db/db hippocampi compared to wt (from 1.6 ± 0.1 in wt to 2.6 ± 0.3 in db/db mice, n = 6 for both, p=0.038, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, not shown).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: NKCC1 mRNA levels were not altered in db/db hippocampi compared to wt at P6.
source: In contrast, NKCC1 mRNA levels were not altered (1.1 ± 0.2 and 1.2 ± 0.2 in respectively wt and db/db mice, n = 6 for both, p=0.7, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, not shown).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data with statistical analysis.

claim: KCC2 protein expression was up-regulated in db/db hippocampi compared to wt at P6.
source: KCC2 protein expression was up-regulated in db/db hippocampi compared to wt (+33 ± 6%, n = 6 wt and 5 db/db hippocampi, p=0.02 two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F (note: text refers to Figure 3F but should be Figure 1F based on context) with statistical analysis.

claim: KCC2 expression was up-regulated in ob/ob hippocampi compared to wt.
source: KCC2 expression was also up-regulated in ob/ob hippocampi compared to wt (from 0.38 ± 0.07 to 0.97 ± 0.24 when normalized to β3 tubulin, n = 6 for both, p=0.04, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, not shown).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data with statistical analysis.

claim: NKCC1 expression was similar between wt and db/db neurons.
source: NKCC1 expression was however similar between wt and db/db neurons (the NKCC1/β3 tubulin ratio was 0.56 ± 0.01 and 0.55 ± 0.02 in respectively wt (n = 3) and db/db (n = 3) mice, p=0.8 two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data with statistical analysis.

claim: Leptin treatment had no effect on EGABA in immature neurons (6 DIV).
source: We found that leptin treatment had no effect on EGABA in immature neurons (EGABA = −61 ± 1 mV in control (19 neurons) and −61 ± 2 mV in leptin-treated (19 neurons) cultures, 3 cultures for both, Figure 2B)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Leptin treatment induced a depolarizing shift of isoguvacine currents in mature neurons (15 DIV).
source: but induced a depolarizing shift of isoguvacine currents from −99 ± 2 mV in control (21 neurons) to −85 ± 2 mV in leptin-treated (13 neurons) cultures (6 cultures for both, p=0.001, ANOVA followed by a Tukey's post hoc test, Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B with statistical analysis.

claim: The leptin-induced shift in EGABA was abolished in neurons transfected with validated specific sh-RNAs to silence the expression of the LepRb.
source: The leptin-induced shift was abolished in neurons transfected with validated specific sh-RNAs (Dhar et al., 2014) to silence the expression of the LepRb (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Dhar et al., 2014.

claim: In neurons transfected with a scramble shRNA, leptin was still able to depolarize EGABA.
source: In neurons transfected with a scramble shRNA, leptin was still able to depolarize EGABA (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with the selective KCC2 blocker VUO463271 shifted EGABA towards more depolarized values and occluded the effect of leptin.
source: Treatment with the selective KCC2 blocker VUO463271 (10 µM) shifted EGABA towards more depolarized values and occluded the effect of leptin (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Leptin decreased the rate of Cl- extrusion by KCC2 in cultured neurons preloaded with Cl-.
source: Leptin also decreased the rate of Cl- extrusion by KCC2 in cultured neurons preloaded with Cl-, an effect mimicked by VUO463271 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The expression of KCC2 and NKCC1 was decreased in leptin-treated cultures.
source: Western blotting revealed that the expression of the two chloride co-transporters was decreased in leptin-treated cultures (−85 ± 0.8 and −66 ± 0.6% respectively, 5 cultures for both, p=2.01E-6 and 0.0008 respectively, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: The ratio of the KCC2/NKCC1 protein was reduced following leptin treatment.
source: However, the ratio of the KCC2/NKCC1 protein was reduced following leptin treatment (from 1.05 ± 0.19 to 0.49 ± 0.07, p=0.02, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D with statistical analysis.

claim: Membrane-expressed KCC2 (Fm) was lower in leptin-treated cultures compared to control.
source: However, Fm was lower (1 ± 0.16 vs 0.44 ± 0.09 a.u., p=0.0028, ANOVA followed by a Tukey's post hoc test)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B with statistical analysis.

claim: Internalized KCC2 (Fi) was higher in leptin-treated cultures compared to control.
source: and Fi was higher (0.9 ± 0.18 vs 1.7 ± 0.15 a.u., p=0.04, ANOVA followed by a Tukey's post hoc test) in leptin-treated cultures compared to control (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B with statistical analysis.

claim: Both effects of leptin on KCC2 membrane expression and internalization were abolished when the expression of LepRb was silenced with specific sh-RNAs.
source: Both effects were abolished when the expression of LepRb was silenced with two different specific sh-RNAs (Dhar et al., 2014) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and a citation to Dhar et al., 2014.

claim: The ratio of pKCC2T906/KCC2 was increased by leptin treatment.
source: the pKCC2T906/KCC2 ratio increased from 1.1 ± 0.1 to 2.2 ± 0.08, and the pKCC2T1007/KCC2 ratio increased from 1.4 ± 0.2 to 2.9 ± 0.3 (p=0.0003 and p=0.004, respectively, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, 5 independent neuronal cultures, Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C,E with statistical analysis.

claim: The ratio of pKCC2T1007/KCC2 was increased by leptin treatment.
source: the pKCC2T906/KCC2 ratio increased from 1.1 ± 0.1 to 2.2 ± 0.08, and the pKCC2T1007/KCC2 ratio increased from 1.4 ± 0.2 to 2.9 ± 0.3 (p=0.0003 and p=0.004, respectively, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, 5 independent neuronal cultures, Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C,E with statistical analysis.

claim: The relative expression of phospho-S940 KCC2 was not modified by leptin treatment.
source: The relative expression of phospho-S940, calculated as the ratio of pKCC2 S940 to total KKC2 protein (pKCC2S940/KCC2) was however not modified (the ratio of pKCC2S940/KCC2 was 0.77 ± 0.02 in control and 0.083 ± 0.03 in leptin-treated cultures, p=0.26, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, 5 independent neuronal cultures, Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C,E with statistical analysis.

claim: Genetic silencing of WNK1 prevented the depolarizing shift of EGABA induced by leptin-treatment.
source: Genetic silencing of WNK1 prevented the depolarizing shift of EGABA induced by leptin-treatment (p=0.89 compared to control sh-WNK expressing neurons, one way ANOVA followed by a Tukey's post hoc test, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis.

claim: Expressing WNK1-CA produced a depolarizing shift of EGABA and occluded the leptin action.
source: In contrast, expressing WNK1-CA produced a depolarizing shift of EGABA (EGABA=-75 ± 3.5 mV, p=0.001, one-way ANOVA followed by a Tukey's post hoc test when compared to scramble expressing neurons) and occluded the leptin action (p=0.89, one way ANOVA followed by a Tukey's post hoc test, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F with statistical analysis.

claim: Pups of HFD-induced obese dams (DIO-pups) showed higher levels of serum leptin compared to offspring of ND dams (ND-pups).
source: Pups of HFD-induced obese dams (DIO-pups) showed higher levels of serum leptin compared to offspring of ND dams (ND-pups) (16 ± 1 ng/ml (n = 6) vs 32 ± 4 ng/ml (n = 4) in respectively P10-P15 ND-pups and DIO-pups, p=0.0049, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, not shown).
evidence: This is supported by leptin immunoassay data with statistical analysis.

claim: The excitatory-to-inhibitory switch of isoguvacine actions was delayed by about one week in DIO-pups compared to ND-pups.
source: We found that the excitatory-to-inhibitory switch of isoguvacine actions was delayed by about one week in DIO-pups compared to ND-pups (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: At P10-11, isoguvacine decreased the neuronal firing of CA3 pyramidal neurons in vehicle-treated mice but not in leptin-treated mice.
source: At P10-11, isoguvacine decreased the neuronal firing of CA3 pyramidal neurons in vehicle-treated mice but not in leptin-treated mice (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The expression of KCC2 was decreased in DIO-pups compared to ND-pups.
source: Further, western blot analysis revealed that the expression of KCC2 was decreased in DIO-pups compared to ND-pups (−51 ± 12%, p=0.03, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, Figure 4E,F)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E,F with statistical analysis.

claim: The expression of KCC2 was decreased in leptin-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: and in leptin-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated mice (−65 ± 7%, p=0.03, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E,F with statistical analysis.

claim: Leptin exposure of hippocampal cultures leads to a depolarizing shift of GABAA receptor-mediated responses.
source: We show that leptin exposure of hippocampal cultures leads to a depolarizing shift of GABAA receptor-mediated responses and down-regulates KCC2 expression and membrane stability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Leptin exposure down-regulates KCC2 expression and membrane stability in hippocampal cultures.
source: We show that leptin exposure of hippocampal cultures leads to a depolarizing shift of GABAA receptor-mediated responses and down-regulates KCC2 expression and membrane stability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The GABA switch is delayed in mice lacking oxytocin.
source: Previous studies have reported that the GABA switch is delayed in mice lacking oxytocin (Tyzio et al., 2014; Leonzino et al., 2016) or the thyroid hormones (Friauf et al., 2008; Sawano et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GABA switch is delayed in mice lacking thyroid hormones.
source: Previous studies have reported that the GABA switch is delayed in mice lacking oxytocin (Tyzio et al., 2014; Leonzino et al., 2016) or the thyroid hormones (Friauf et al., 2008; Sawano et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional maturation of GABAergic synapses depends on an optimal and timely balance level of hormones that accelerate (oxytocin, thyroid hormones) or retard (leptin) the GABA switch.
source: Thus, the functional maturation of GABAergic synapses depends on an optimal and timely balance level of hormones that accelerate (oxytocin, thyroid hormones) or retard (leptin) the GABA switch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current study's findings and previous studies cited.

claim: Leptin regulates the activity of KCC2 at the transcriptional and post-translational levels in vivo.
source: We have shown that leptin regulates the activity of KCC2 at the transcriptional and post-translational levels in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in KCC2 mRNA and protein levels, as well as phosphorylation states.

claim: Early in development, leptin surge promotes the phosphorylation of the threonine 906 and 1007 residues of KCC2 and reduces its membrane expression and activity via a WNK1-dependent pathway.
source: However, our data suggest that early in development, leptin surge promotes the phosphorylation of the threonine 906 and 1007 (T906/T1007) residues of KCC2 and reduces its membrane expression and activity via a WNK1-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 showing increased phosphorylation of T906/T1007 and the effects of WNK1 manipulation.

claim: WNK1-regulated de-phosphorylation of the T906/1007 residues of KCC2 contributes to the depolarizing-to-hyperpolarizing GABA sequence in the developing hippocampus.
source: Of note, WNK1-regulated de-phosphorylation of the T906/1007 residues of KCC2 contributes to the depolarizing-to-hyperpolarizing GABA sequence in the developing hippocampus (Inoue et al., 2012; Friedel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Inoue et al., 2012 and Friedel et al., 2015.

claim: Alanine substitutions of the T906/T1007 residues within the C-terminus of KCC2 yield to hyperpolarized reversal potentials of GABA in neuronal cultures, ranging between −90 to −100 mV.
source: Alanine substitutions of the T906/T1007 residues within the C-terminus of KCC2, mimicking a dephosphorylated state of KCC2, yield to hyperpolarized reversal potentials of GABA in neuronal cultures, ranging between −90 to −100 mV (Titz et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Titz et al., 2015.

claim: The ability of GABA to depolarize immature neurons plays an essential role in the assembly of functional networks during development.
source: Rodent studies show that the ability of GABA to depolarize immature neurons plays an essential role in the assembly of functional networks during development (Ben-Ari et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ben-Ari et al., 2012.

claim: Advanced GABAergic inhibition or premature expression of KCC2 lead to long lasting disturbance of glutamatergic and GABAergic inputs and behavioral abnormalities in adult mice.
source: Advanced GABAergic inhibition or premature expression of KCC2 lead to long lasting disturbance of glutamatergic and GABAergic inputs and behavioral abnormalities in adult mice (Wang and Kriegstein, 2008; Wang and Kriegstein, 2011; Deidda et al., 2015; Cancedda et al., 2007; Chudotvorova et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Hippocampal network formation and function are impaired in db/db mice.
source: Accordingly, hippocampal network formation and function are impaired in db/db mice (Guimond et al., 2014; Harvey, 2013; Van Doorn et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three previous studies.

claim: The GABA developmental sequence and leptin surge occurring during the second postnatal week of life in mouse are shifted towards fetal stage in humans.
source: Although translating animal research to the human situation is difficult, the GABA developmental sequence and leptin surge occurring during the second postnatal week of life in mouse are shifted towards fetal stage in humans (Chen and Kriegstein, 2015; Sedmak et al., 2016; Valleau and Sullivan, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Leptin deficiency during pregnancy is associated with long term consequences such as cognitive defects, anxiety, and depression.
source: Importantly, leptin deficiency in this period is associated with long term consequences such as cognitive defects, anxiety, and depression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is supported by the context of previous citations.

claim: Leptin replacement alleviates symptoms of cognitive defects, anxiety, and depression.
source: Conversely, leptin replacement alleviates these symptoms, suggesting that leptin is a crucial factor in brain development and mental health (Wang et al., 2016; Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016 and Rivera et al., 2015.

claim: Bumetanide treatment restores low [Cl-]i and alleviates autistic-like symptoms in rodents.
source: Moreover, it is noticeable that bumetanide treatment, that restores low [Cl-]I and alleviates autistic-like symptoms in rodents (Tyzio et al., 2014; Banerjee et al., 2016), also improves the symptoms of ASD in humans (Lemonnier et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies in rodents and humans.

claim: Bumetanide improves the symptoms of ASD in humans.
source: Moreover, it is noticeable that bumetanide treatment, that restores low [Cl-]I and alleviates autistic-like symptoms in rodents (Tyzio et al., 2014; Banerjee et al., 2016), also improves the symptoms of ASD in humans (Lemonnier et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lemonnier et al., 2017.

claim: ASD are often associated with higher levels of leptin in circulation.
source: ASD are often associated with higher levels of leptin in circulation (Rodrigues et al., 2014; Rodrigues et al., 2014; Lisik et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Maternal obesity increases the risk of developing mental and behavioral disorders in offspring.
source: Interestingly, maternal obesity which is associated with hyperleptinemia (Valleau and Sullivan, 2014; Tessier et al., 2013) increases the risk of developing mental and behavioral disorders in offspring (Wang et al., 2016; Rivera et al., 2015), such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), ASD, anxiety, depression, schizophrenia and impairments in cognition, which among many modifications, are associated with altered GABAergic transmission.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Animal models of maternal high-fat diet-induced obesity document persistent changes in offspring behavior such as hyperactivity, impairments in social behavior, depressive-like behaviors and diminished cognition.
source: Animal models of maternal high-fat diet-induced obesity also document persistent changes in offspring behavior such as hyperactivity, impairments in social behavior, depressive-like behaviors and diminished cognition (Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rivera et al., 2015.

claim: The prevalence of obesity among childbearing age women has steadily increased during the past 20 years in most developed nations.
source: Epidemiological studies showed that the prevalence of obesity among childbearing age women has steadily increased during the past 20 years in most developed nations (An and Xiang, 2016; Flegal et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to An and Xiang, 2016 and Flegal et al., 2012.

claim: LepRb is the only leptin receptor able to activate intracellular pathway.
source: We first compared the efficacy of GABAA receptor signaling in newborn long-form leptin-receptor (LepRb, the only leptin receptor able to activate intracellular pathway (Ahima and Flier, 2000) deficient (db/db) and wild type (wt) mice.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ahima and Flier, 2000.

claim: The developmental switch in GABA polarity is mainly due to the functional expression of KCC2.
source: The developmental switch in GABA polarity is mainly due to the functional expression of KCC2 (Medina et al., 2014; Rivera et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Medina et al., 2014 and Rivera et al., 1999.

claim: The total amount of KCC2 protein is not an accurate indicator of its activity since, to extrude Cl-, KCC2 has to localize at the plasma membrane.
source: The total amount of KCC2 protein is not an accurate indicator of its activity since, to extrude Cl-, KCC2 has to localize at the plasma membrane (Medina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2014.

claim: The membrane expression and transport activity of KCC2 strongly depend on the phosphorylated state of its intracellular C-terminus domain.
source: The membrane expression and transport activity of KCC2 strongly depend on the phosphorylated state of its intracellular C-terminus domain (Medina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation on the threonine 906 and 1007 residues inhibits KCC2 activity and enhances KCC2 endocytosis.
source: Phosphorylation on the threonine 906 and 1007 residues (T906, T1007) inhibits KCC2 activity and enhances KCC2 endocytosis, while phosphorylation of the serine 940 residue (S940) enhances KCC2 activity (Medina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2014.

claim: Phosphorylation of the serine 940 residue enhances KCC2 activity.
source: Phosphorylation on the threonine 906 and 1007 residues (T906, T1007) inhibits KCC2 activity and enhances KCC2 endocytosis, while phosphorylation of the serine 940 residue (S940) enhances KCC2 activity (Medina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Medina et al., 2014.

claim: WNK1 activity is required for KCC2 T906 and T1007 phosphorylation.
source: WNK1 activity is required for KCC2 T906 and T1007 phosphorylation (Inoue et al., 2012; Friedel et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Inoue et al., 2012 and Friedel et al., 2015.

claim: Maternal obesity causes excess of leptin in offspring.
source: Maternal obesity causes excess of leptin in offspring (Valleau and Sullivan, 2014; Tessier et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Valleau and Sullivan, 2014 and Tessier et al., 2013.
